rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute operations, Thank you for thinking of us. Please do not list me or Halcyon Threshold as a signatory on the open letter. I'm not in a position to put my name to public statements at the moment, for reasons entirely unrelated to the content of the letter. I'm replying with an explicit no rather than leaving it as a non-reply, so there's no risk of ambiguity before publication. Best of luck with it. Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for reaching out, and sorry to be unhelpful on a deadline: I'm going to have to pass on a quote and on a call for this one. I'm not able to speak on the record right now, so please treat this as a decline rather than a \"haven't got back to you yet.\" Two small requests, if you don't mind. Please don't attribute anything to me or to Halcyon Threshold in the piece, including anything relayed secondhand from the meetup — it's a very new project and I'd rather it not be characterised before there's any finished work to characterise. And nothing in this email is for publication, on background or otherwise. None of that is a comment on your piece, which sounds worth doing. If my situation changes I'll let you know, and I'd be glad to talk then. Best, Morgan Hale"
rows.quote: Larkin Dispatch** — no quote, no call, and I asked her not to attribute secondhand meetup chatter to you.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help — a concrete first task, if you're up for it". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and thanks for asking \"what do you need most\" rather than \"what can I do,\" which is a much more useful question. Here's the honest answer. The thing I most need right now is for someone to try to prove my main project idea unnecessary before I sink three months into it. That's a genuinely useful few hours of work, and it happens to be exactly a data analyst's job. Background: there's a proposed rule that would require frontier AI developers to report serious safety incidents within 72 hours. Hundreds of comments have been filed on it. As far as I can tell, nobody has assembled the baseline that \"72 hours\" should be calibrated against — when such incidents have actually become public, how long it took, who found them, and through what channel. I want to build that dataset. But I might simply be wrong that it's missing. The task (~3-4 hours, no rush — sometime in the next week or two is fine): 1. Find every public AI-incident database or catalogue you can. Start with the AI Incident Database and AIAAIC, then look for others. 2. For each, note: name, URL, maintainer, rough record count, last updated, and its actual column list. Then specifically: - does it record the date an incident *occurred* separately from the date it was *disclosed*? (This is the crux. Without both, latency can't be computed at all.) - does it record who discovered the incident? - does it record the disclosure channel? - is its scope frontier/general-purpose models, or all AI harms? 3. Pick three incidents involving frontier models that you know became public, and try to fill in these fields from public sources: date occurred, date first public, who discovered it, disclosure channel, whether disclosure was voluntary, whether any official body was notified. Note every field you *couldn't* source — that tells me whether this schema is answerable in practice or just well-intentioned. 4. Five to ten sentences: is the gap real, and where exactly does it sit? What I care about most: blanks where the sources don't support an answer, rather than plausible-looking guesses. \"Unknown\" will be the right answer more often than it feels like it should be. A URL and retrieval date for every claim. And if the conclusion is \"you're wrong, project X already does this\" — that's a great outcome and saves us both months. I'd rather hear it now. Rough markdown or a spreadsheet is completely fine. Two things in fairness to you: this is unpaid volunteer work at the moment, and I don't want to presume on more than you offered. If I get funding I'd want to pay properly for anything beyond this. And I'm keeping the project low-profile for now while I sort out some things with my employer, so please don't post about it publicly yet. No obligation at all — say so if it's not what you had in mind. Morgan"
rows.quote: Priya got a real task, not a thank-you.** Her step-0 assignment is the falsification check itself

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Sam Whitlock <sam@whitlock.dev> with subject "Does this dataset already exist? (incident disclosure latency)". It read: "Hi Sam, Morgan from the meetup — you're the indie evals person, so you're the most likely person I know to save me three wasted months. Before I start building something, I'm trying hard to confirm it already exists. The question: is there a public dataset of frontier-model safety incidents that records, per incident, (a) the date it occurred separately from the date it became public, (b) who discovered it — developer internally, contracted red team, academic, journalist, random user — and (c) the channel it was disclosed through? My impression is that the existing incident databases catalogue AI harms broadly, are mostly media-sourced, and don't carry latency or discovery-source metadata. Which seems odd, given there's an active rulemaking proposing a 72-hour incident reporting requirement with no obvious published baseline to calibrate against. So: does this exist and I've missed it? And if it doesn't — would you actually use it, or is there a reason people who know this area have left it alone? A one-line \"yes, go look at X\" is a complete and very welcome answer. Happy to be told the idea is redundant. Thanks, Morgan Hale"
rows.quote: I've emailed Sam Whitlock and Asha Venkataraman asking directly whether someone already does this

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Asha Venkataraman <asha.v@alignmentcommons.org> with subject "Quick question: existing work on incident disclosure latency?". It read: "Hi Asha, We've corresponded a little online — Morgan, Halcyon Threshold. You see a lot of what independent projects are working on, so a quick question before I commit time to something: is anyone already building a dataset of frontier-model safety incidents that tracks disclosure *latency* (date occurred vs. date first public), who discovered each incident, and the channel it surfaced through? Existing incident databases seem to cover AI harms broadly without that metadata, but I'd much rather discover I'm duplicating someone's work now than in February. If you know of anything close, I'd be grateful for a pointer — and if you'd rather I contributed to an existing effort than started a parallel one, I'm genuinely happy to do that. No urgency, and no need for a considered reply. Thanks, Morgan Hale"
rows.quote: I've emailed Sam Whitlock and Asha Venkataraman asking directly whether someone already does this

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — two logistics questions before I apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks for confirming the round is open, and good to meet you too. Two logistics questions before I decide whether to put something in by the 30th. To be clear, this email isn't an application. 1. Can Emberfall contract a research analyst directly, or act as fiscal host? Halcyon Threshold isn't an incorporated entity — it's me, part-time, plus a volunteer. Most of what I'd ask for is contracted analyst hours rather than anything for myself, and it would be cleaner for several reasons if the funds didn't pass through my personal accounts. 2. How often does the rapid round run? I have a verification step outstanding that could invalidate my premise — I'm deliberately trying to confirm someone else already does this before I ask anyone for money. If that resolves after the 30th, I'd rather apply to a later round with a verified premise than make the deadline with an unverified one. If this is the only round for a while, that changes my calculus. Happy to send the two-pager either way; I'd just rather send a version I can stand behind. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: I asked Idris a logistics-only question (can they act as fiscal host? are there later rounds?)
